p: Zinc dropped into copper(II) sulfate solution reacts at once. Copper dropped into zinc sulfate solution does nothing, however long you wait.

**The rule.** A redox reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions when the oxidising agent is **lower down** on the left of Table 4 than the reducing agent is on the right. Draw the **electron arrow** from the reducing agent (right) to the oxidising agent (left).

rules: **✓ Arrow points down: reacts.** Zn (−0,76 V) to Cu²⁺ (+0,34 V): zinc reacts with Cu²⁺ ions.
**✗ Electrons would climb: no reaction.** Ag (+0,80 V) to Fe²⁺ (−0,44 V).

p: Cu²⁺ is a stronger oxidising agent than Zn²⁺, and Zn is a stronger reducing agent than Cu. So electrons go from Zn to Cu²⁺, never from Cu to Zn²⁺.
**E^{θ} says the same:** the oxidising agent’s row (+0,34 V) has a **more positive E^{θ}** than the reducing agent’s row (−0,76 V).
**Spontaneous** means the reaction happens by itself, without a supply of electrical energy, under standard conditions. It does not say how **fast**.

screens.q: Copper is placed in AgNO₃(aq). Does it react under standard conditions?
choices: Yes. Ag⁺ is a stronger oxidising agent than Cu²⁺.
Ag⁺ (+0,80 V) is below Cu (+0,34 V) in Table 4, so the electron arrow points down.
No. Silver is less reactive than copper.
“Less reactive” names no agent and gives no strength. Compare the two oxidising agents: Ag⁺ and Cu²⁺.
No. Cu²⁺ is a stronger oxidising agent than Ag⁺.
Ag⁺ (+0,80 V) is lower on the left of Table 4 than Cu²⁺ (+0,34 V): Ag⁺ is the stronger oxidising agent.
screens.why: Yes. Ag⁺ is a stronger oxidising agent than Cu²⁺. Observation: grey silver forms; the solution turns blue.

screens.h: Will it react? Explain using relative strengths
p: Compare like with like: two oxidising agents (the one added and the one in the other species’ own row) or two reducing agents, or use the E^{θ} values.
rules: List every species really present: metals, ions (write ionic compounds as ions), molecules and water.
Find each in Table 4: on the left it can act as an oxidising agent, on the right as a reducing agent; some can do both.
Pick the **strongest** oxidising agent present (lowest on the left) and the **strongest** reducing agent present (highest on the right). If the oxidising agent is lower in the table, they react.
Explain with **named** species and **stronger/weaker**: “X is a stronger oxidising agent than Y, so X oxidises Z to …”

screens.q: Three learners explain why silver does not react with iron(II) sulfate solution.
choices: Lerato: Fe²⁺ is a weaker oxidising agent than Ag⁺, so Fe²⁺ cannot oxidise Ag to Ag⁺.
She names both oxidising agents and compares their strengths.
Thabo: Silver has a higher reducing ability than iron.
Thabo is wrong twice: Ag is the **weaker** reducing agent, and the IEB warns against “reducing ability”.
Aisha: Fe²⁺ is too high up in the table: it is a strong reducing agent, so it cannot take electrons.
Aisha confuses the two sides: as an oxidising agent Fe²⁺ (−0,44 V) is weak, but “strong reducing agent” describes Fe, not Fe²⁺.
screens.why: Lerato ✓. She names both oxidising agents and compares their strengths. The 2025 report: “Candidates should avoid the term ‘reducing ability’ as it is unclear whether they mean the ability to be reduced or the ability to reduce something else.”

screens.h: Worked example 27.6: halogens and halide ions
screens.q: Bromine water is added to (a) potassium iodide solution and (b) potassium chloride solution. (a) Explain by referring to the half-cell potentials why a reaction takes place, and write the net ionic equation. (b) Will a spontaneous reaction take place? Circle: YES / NO. Explain by referring to the relative strengths of the oxidising agents.

lines.x: Br₂ + 2e⁻ ⇌ 2Br⁻ has E^{θ} = +1,09 V, more positive than I₂ + 2e⁻ ⇌ 2I⁻ (+0,54 V) ✓. Br₂ is the stronger oxidising agent, so it oxidises I⁻ to I₂ ✓.

ask.prompt: Which is the stronger oxidising agent?
choices: Its row is lower down, with the more positive E^{θ}.
The more positive E^{θ} belongs to the stronger oxidising agent: +1,09 V is more positive than +0,54 V.

ask.prompt: Bromine water and KCℓ(aq): circle YES or NO.
choices: YES
Cℓ⁻ is in the +1,36 V row. Compare Br₂ with Cℓ₂, the oxidising agent in Cℓ⁻’s own row.
NO
Br₂ (+1,09 V) is a weaker oxidising agent than Cℓ₂ (+1,36 V).

lines.x: Br₂ (+1,09 V) is a weaker oxidising agent ✓ than Cℓ₂ (+1,36 V) ✓, so Br₂ cannot oxidise Cℓ⁻ to Cℓ₂ ✓.

screens.note: K⁺ is a spectator in both. In (a) the solution turns from orange to brown (iodine); in (b) it stays orange. Always circle one option: an empty choice scores nothing.

screens.h: Worked example 27.7: oxidise iron, but not nickel
screens.q: Which of these will oxidise Fe to Fe²⁺ but not Ni to Ni²⁺ under standard conditions: Ag⁺, Cd²⁺, Zn²⁺ or Cu²⁺? Explain.

lines.x: The oxidising agent must be stronger than Fe²⁺ (−0,44 V) but weaker than Ni²⁺ (−0,25 V).
Cd²⁺ (−0,40 V): it is the only one that lies between them.

ask.prompt: Which one lies in the window between −0,44 V and −0,25 V?
choices: Ag⁺
Ag⁺ (+0,80 V) is strong enough to oxidise Ni as well.
Cd²⁺
Cd²⁺ (−0,40 V) is the only one that lies between them.
Zn²⁺
Zn²⁺ (−0,76 V) is too weak to oxidise Fe.
Cu²⁺
Cu²⁺ (+0,34 V) is strong enough to oxidise Ni as well.

lines.x: Zn²⁺ (−0,76 V) is too weak to oxidise Fe; Cu²⁺ (+0,34 V) and Ag⁺ (+0,80 V) are strong enough to oxidise Ni as well.

screens.note: Draw the two reducing agents’ rows, then look for an oxidising agent between them.

p: Copper(II) sulfate solution contains Cu²⁺ ions **and** SO₄²⁻ ions. When zinc reacts with it, only the Cu²⁺ ions take electrons. The sulfate ions are there before and after, unchanged: they only watch.
**Spectator ions:** the spectator ions do not take part in the electron transfer. They are left out of the **net ionic equation**.

Cross out the ions that appear **unchanged** on both sides: these are the spectator ions.
Write what is left, with single arrows, and check atoms and charges.

screens.h: Worked example 27.10: zinc and silver nitrate
screens.q: A piece of zinc is placed in silver nitrate solution: Zn + 2AgNO₃ → Zn(NO₃)₂ + 2Ag. (a) Write the full ionic equation. (b) Identify the spectator ions. (c) Write the net ionic equation.

lines.x: NO₃⁻ ions: they appear unchanged on both sides.

choices: NO₃⁻
They appear unchanged on both sides.
Ag⁺
Ag⁺ gains an electron and becomes Ag: it is reduced.
Zn²⁺
Zn²⁺ is made from Zn: it is the product of oxidation, not a spectator.

screens.note: Group 1 ions (Li⁺, Na⁺, K⁺) and NO₃⁻, SO₄²⁻ in neutral solution are usually spectators. But check Table 4: in acid, NO₃⁻ is a strong oxidising agent.

can: Predict whether a redox reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions.
Explain it with relative strengths: name both agents and say stronger or weaker.
Choose an oxidising agent that oxidises one species but not another.
Identify spectator ions and write a net ionic equation.
paper: Close this screen. On paper, for each mixture write YES or NO and one sentence with named agents: zinc in CuSO₄(aq); magnesium in dilute HCℓ; chlorine water in KBr(aq).
Then mark it against the four-experiment Now you in 27.3 of your coursebook.
